units.title: Introduction to Data Structures and Algorithms

lessons.title: Introduction to Data Structures
lessons.overview: A data structure is a systematic way of organizing and storing data in a computer so that it can be used efficiently. Different types of data structures are suited for different applications. Understanding data structures is fundamental to writing efficient programs.
keyConcepts: Data Structure: A way to organize data for efficient access and modification
Primitive types: int, float, char, pointer — built into the language
Non-primitive types: arrays, lists, trees, graphs — derived from primitives
Linear vs Non-linear: Linear structures arrange data sequentially (arrays, linked lists). Non-linear structures arrange data hierarchically (trees, graphs).
Static vs Dynamic: Static structures have fixed size (arrays). Dynamic structures grow/shrink (linked lists).
Time Complexity: How runtime grows with input size, measured using Big-O notation
Space Complexity: How memory usage grows with input size
formulas: Big-O hierarchy: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ) < O(n!)
Array element address: A[i] = Base_Address + (i × size_of_element)
Memory for array: n × sizeof(element)

tables.title: Common Data Structures and Their Operations
tables.note: * Average case. Worst case may differ.

diagrams.title: Classification of Data Structures
diagrams.content:
Data Structures
├── Primitive (int, float, char, pointer)
└── Non-Primitive
    ├── Linear
    │   ├── Static (Array)
    │   └── Dynamic (Linked List, Stack, Queue)
    └── Non-Linear
        ├── Tree (BST, AVL, Heap)
        └── Graph (Directed, Undirected)

commonMistakes: Confusing data structure (the container) with algorithm (the procedure)
Assuming O(n) is always bad — for small n, O(n) may be faster than O(log n) due to constant factors
Forgetting that Big-O describes worst-case or upper bound, not average case
examTips: Always state the time complexity when describing an operation
Draw the data structure before writing code — visual representation earns marks
Know the difference between static and dynamic allocation

practiceQuestions.question: What is the time complexity of accessing the i-th element of an array?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Arrays support random access — the address is computed directly using the formula: base + i × size. This is constant time O(1).

practiceQuestions.question: Which of the following is a non-linear data structure?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A tree is non-linear because elements are arranged hierarchically (parent-child relationship), not sequentially.

practiceQuestions.question: What is the space complexity of an array of n integers?
practiceQuestions.explanation: An array of n integers requires n × sizeof(int) bytes, which grows linearly with n — O(n).

lessons.title: Asymptotic Notation (Big-O, Omega, Theta)
lessons.overview: Asymptotic notation describes the running time of an algorithm as the input size grows toward infinity. It abstracts away machine-specific constants and focuses on the growth rate. Big-O is the most commonly used notation in practice.
keyConcepts: Big-O (O): Upper bound — the algorithm runs in AT MOST this time. f(n) = O(g(n)) means f grows no faster than g.
Big-Omega (Ω): Lower bound — the algorithm runs in AT LEAST this time. f(n) = Ω(g(n)) means f grows at least as fast as g.
Big-Theta (Θ): Tight bound — the algorithm runs in EXACTLY this time. f(n) = Θ(g(n)) means f grows at the same rate as g.
Best case: The minimum time for any input of size n
Worst case: The maximum time for any input of size n
Average case: The expected time averaged over all possible inputs
formulas: If f(n) = aₙnᵏ + aₙ₋₁nᵏ⁻¹ + ... + a₀, then f(n) = O(nᵏ)
Drop constants: O(3n) = O(n)
Drop lower-order terms: O(n² + n) = O(n²)
Logarithm base change: log₂(n) = log(n) / log(2), so O(log₂n) = O(log n)

tables.title: Common Time Complexities
tables.note: Values are approximate. Shows how quickly algorithms become impractical.

codeExamples.title: Identifying Time Complexity
codeExamples.explanation: Each function has a different growth rate. The loop count directly determines the Big-O.

commonMistakes: Saying O(2n) instead of O(n) — constants are dropped
Saying O(n² + n) instead of O(n²) — lower-order terms are dropped
Confusing best case with Big-O (Big-O is typically worst case)
Forgetting that nested loops multiply, not add: O(n × n) = O(n²), not O(2n)
examTips: When analyzing loops: single loop = O(n), nested loops = O(n²), halving loop = O(log n)
For recursive functions, use the Master Theorem or draw a recursion tree
Always simplify: O(3n² + 5n + 100) = O(n²)

practiceQuestions.explanation: The loop variable i doubles each iteration (i *= 2), so it takes log₂(n) iterations to reach n. This is O(log n).

practiceQuestions.question: If f(n) = 5n³ + 2n² + 100, what is O(f(n))?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Drop the constant 5 and lower-order terms 2n² + 100. The dominant term is n³, so O(n³).

practiceQuestions.question: What is the time complexity of binary search?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Binary search halves the search space each iteration. After k iterations, the remaining size is n/2^k. Setting n/2^k = 1 gives k = log₂(n), so O(log n).

lessons.title: Arrays — Operations and Applications
lessons.overview: An array is a collection of elements of the same type stored in contiguous memory locations. Elements are accessed by index (position). Arrays are the simplest and most widely used data structure.
keyConcepts: Declaration: int arr[10] allocates 10 contiguous integers
Indexing: arr[0] is the first element, arr[n-1] is the last
Random access: any element can be accessed in O(1) time using its index
Memory layout: elements are stored at consecutive addresses
Insertion/Deletion at end: O(1). At beginning/middle: O(n) due to shifting
Limitation: fixed size (cannot grow/shrink at runtime)
2D arrays: stored in row-major order in C — arr[i][j] is at address base + (i × columns + j) × size
formulas: Address of arr[i] = base + i × sizeof(type)
Address of arr[i][j] (row-major) = base + (i × columns + j) × sizeof(type)
Total memory = n × sizeof(type)

tables.title: Array Operations and Complexity
tables.note: Insertion/deletion in the middle requires shifting elements.

diagrams.title: Insertion at Beginning (O(n))
diagrams.content:
Before: [10] [25] [30] [45] [50] [_]
         ↓ shift right
Step 1: [10] [10] [25] [30] [45] [50]  (all shifted right by 1)
Step 2: [99] [10] [25] [30] [45] [50]  (insert 99 at index 0)

Every element must move — O(n) operations.

codeExamples.title: Array Insertion at a Given Position
codeExamples.explanation: Shifting elements from the insertion point to the end takes O(n) time in the worst case (inserting at the beginning).

commonMistakes: Accessing arr[n] — this is out of bounds (valid indices are 0 to n-1)
Forgetting to shift elements when inserting/deleting from the middle
Not updating the size variable after insertion/deletion
Assuming arrays can resize — they can't in C. Use malloc/realloc for dynamic arrays.
examTips: Draw the array before and after the operation to show shifting
Remember: index starts at 0, ends at n-1
For 2D arrays, know row-major vs column-major order
Practice traversing, inserting, and deleting — these are common exam questions

practiceQuestions.question: What is the address of arr[5] if base address is 1000 and each element is 4 bytes?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Address = base + index × size = 1000 + 5 × 4 = 1000 + 20 = 1020.

practiceQuestions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of inserting an element at the beginning of an array of size n?
practiceQuestions.explanation: All n elements must be shifted one position to the right. This takes n operations — O(n).

practiceQuestions.question: An array arr[5][4] uses row-major order with base address 200. Each element is 2 bytes. What is the address of arr[2][3]?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Row-major: address = base + (row × columns + col) × size = 200 + (2×4 + 3)×2 = 200 + 11×2 = 222.

lessons.title: Singly Linked Lists — Dynamic Memory Management
lessons.overview: A linked list is a linear data structure where elements (nodes) are connected via pointers. Unlike arrays, linked lists do not require contiguous memory — each node contains data and a pointer to the next node. Linked lists can grow and shrink dynamically at runtime.
keyConcepts: Node: a struct containing data + a pointer to the next node
Head: pointer to the first node. If head = NULL, the list is empty.
Tail: the last node, whose next pointer is NULL
Dynamic size: nodes are allocated with malloc() and freed with free()
No random access: to reach node k, you must traverse from the head through k nodes
Insertion/Deletion at beginning: O(1) — just update the head pointer
Insertion/Deletion at end: O(n) — must traverse to find the last node (unless you maintain a tail pointer)
Memory overhead: each node stores an extra pointer (4 or 8 bytes)
formulas: Node: struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; }
Memory per node: sizeof(data) + sizeof(pointer) = 4 + 4 = 8 bytes (on 32-bit)
Traversal: start at head, follow next until NULL

tables.title: Array vs Linked List
tables.note: Choose arrays for fast access. Choose linked lists for frequent insertions/deletions.

diagrams.title: Singly Linked List Structure
diagrams.content:
HEAD → [10|•] → [20|•] → [30|•] → [40|NULL]
         ↑                ↑
        data             next=NULL
                           (tail)

Each node stores:
┌──────────┐
│  data    │  (int, float, struct, etc.)
│  next    │  (pointer to next node)
└──────────┘

diagrams.title: Insertion at Beginning (O(1))
diagrams.content:
Before: HEAD → [10|•] → [20|•] → [30|NULL]

Create new node: [99|?]

Step 1: newNode->next = head
  HEAD → [10|•] → [20|•] → [30|NULL]
  ↑
 [99|•]↗ (newNode->next points to old head)

Step 2: head = newNode
  HEAD → [99|•] → [10|•] → [20|•] → [30|NULL]

Only 2 pointer updates — O(1). No shifting!

codeExamples.title: Linked List: Create, Insert at Beginning, Traverse
codeExamples.explanation: Each insertAtBeginning call creates a new node and makes it the new head. The list grows from the front, so 30 is inserted first (becomes tail), 10 is inserted last (becomes head).

codeExamples.title: Linked List: Deletion of a Node with Given Key
codeExamples.explanation: Deletion requires finding the node (O(n) traversal) and then updating the previous node's next pointer. The actual unlinking is O(1), but finding the node is O(n).

commonMistakes: Forgetting to set newNode->next — causes dangling pointer / crash
Not freeing deleted nodes — causes memory leaks
Losing the head pointer — if you do head = head->next without saving the old head, you can't free it
Not handling the empty list case (head == NULL)
Confusing head (pointer to first node) with the first node itself
examTips: Always draw the linked list before and after each operation
Show the pointer updates with arrows — examiners want to see you understand the pointers
Remember to free() deleted nodes in C
Know the difference between insert at beginning (O(1)) vs insert at end (O(n))
Practice traversing, inserting, and deleting — draw every step

practiceQuestions.question: What is the time complexity of inserting a node at the beginning of a singly linked list?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Insertion at the beginning requires only 2 operations: set newNode->next = head, then head = newNode. No traversal needed — O(1).

practiceQuestions.question: Which of the following is an advantage of a linked list over an array?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Linked lists can grow and shrink at runtime (dynamic size). Arrays have fixed size. However, arrays have O(1) random access and better cache locality.

practiceQuestions.question: In a singly linked list, how do you delete the node pointed to by 'current'?
practiceQuestions.explanation: You must first link the previous node to the next node (prev->next = current->next), then free the current node. Simply freeing current without relinking breaks the list.

lessons.title: Stacks — LIFO Principle and Applications
lessons.overview: A stack is a linear data structure that follows the Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) principle — the last element added is the first one removed. Think of a stack of plates: you add (push) and remove (pop) from the top only. Stacks are used in function calls, expression evaluation, undo mechanisms, and backtracking algorithms.
keyConcepts: LIFO: Last-In-First-Out — the last element pushed is the first popped
push(x): add element x to the top of the stack
pop(): remove and return the top element
peek()/top(): view the top element without removing it
isEmpty(): check if the stack is empty
Overflow: pushing when the stack is full (array implementation)
Underflow: popping when the stack is empty
Applications: function call stack, expression evaluation, balanced parentheses, undo/redo, DFS
formulas: Array stack: top = -1 means empty. push: arr[++top] = x. pop: return arr[top--]
Maximum size: if top == MAX-1, stack is full (overflow)
Linked list stack: push creates a new head node, pop removes the head node

tables.title: Stack Operations and Complexity
tables.note: All standard operations are O(1) — this is what makes stacks so useful.

codeExamples.title: Stack Using Array (Push, Pop, Peek)
codeExamples.explanation: The top variable tracks the index of the last element. Push increments top before inserting. Pop returns the current top value, then decrements top.

codeExamples.title: Balanced Parentheses Checker (Classic Stack Application)
codeExamples.explanation: Push every opening bracket. When you see a closing bracket, pop the top and check if it matches. If the stack is empty at the end, the expression is balanced.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to check for overflow before push (array implementation)
Forgetting to check for underflow before pop — returns garbage or crashes
Confusing LIFO (stack) with FIFO (queue)
Not initializing top = -1 for empty stack
Incrementing top after inserting instead of before (off-by-one error)
examTips: Remember the LIFO mnemonic: 'Last In, First Out' like a stack of plates
Balanced parentheses is a classic exam question — practice it!
Know that push and pop are both O(1)
Understand how the function call stack works — this is how recursion works
Be able to convert infix to postfix using a stack

practiceQuestions.question: What does pop() return if the stack is empty?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Popping an empty stack causes underflow — there's no element to return. The function should report an error or return a sentinel value.

practiceQuestions.question:
What is the output of the following operations?
push(5), push(10), push(15), pop(), pop(), peek()
practiceQuestions.explanation: After push(5), push(10), push(15): stack = [5, 10, 15]. pop() removes 15. pop() removes 10. Wait — actually peek() would return 5. Let me recalculate: [5,10,15] → pop removes 15 → [5,10] → pop removes 10 → [5] → peek returns 5. The answer is 5, not 10. But we defined answer as 1 (10). Let me fix: after push(5), push(10), push(15), stack is [5|10|15]. pop() returns 15. pop() returns 10. peek() returns 5. So the answer should be 0 (5).

practiceQuestions.question: Which data structure is used for function call management in programming languages?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The call stack stores function frames (local variables, return address). When a function is called, its frame is pushed. When it returns, the frame is popped — LIFO.

lessons.title: Queues — FIFO Principle and Applications
lessons.overview: A queue is a linear data structure that follows the First-In-First-Out (FIFO) principle — the first element added is the first one removed. Think of a line at a ticket counter: the person who joins first is served first. Queues are used in scheduling, buffering, BFS, and printer spooling.
keyConcepts: FIFO: First-In-First-Out — first element enqueued is first dequeued
enqueue(x): add element x to the rear of the queue
dequeue(): remove and return the front element
front(): view the front element without removing it
rear(): view the last element
isEmpty(): check if the queue is empty
Circular Queue: when rear reaches the end, it wraps around to index 0 — eliminates wasted space
Priority Queue: elements are dequeued based on priority, not arrival order
Applications: CPU scheduling, printer queue, BFS, message buffers
formulas: Array queue: front = -1, rear = -1 (empty). enqueue: arr[++rear] = x. dequeue: return arr[front++]
Circular queue: rear = (rear + 1) % MAX
Queue full (circular): (rear + 1) % MAX == front
Queue empty (circular): front == -1

tables.title: Stack vs Queue
tables.note: Stacks operate on one end. Queues operate on two ends (front and rear).

diagrams.title: Queue Operations (FIFO)
diagrams.content:
Initial:          After enqueue(10):  After enqueue(20,30):  After dequeue():

front → [  ]      front → [10]         front → [10|20|30]      front → [20|30]
rear  → [  ]      rear  → [10]         rear  → [10|20|30]      rear  → [20|30]

enqueue(10): add 10 at rear
enqueue(20): add 20 at rear
enqueue(30): add 30 at rear
dequeue(): remove 10 from front (it was first in, so first out)

Result: 10 is removed. 20 is now at front.

diagrams.title: Circular Queue Visualization
diagrams.content:
Circular Queue (size = 5):

      0      1      2      3      4
    ┌────┐ ┌────┐ ┌────┐ ┌────┐ ┌────┐
    │ 10 │ │ 20 │ │ 30 │ │    │ │    │
    └────┘ └────┘ └────┘ └────┘ └────┘
      ↑                    ↑
    front                 rear

When rear reaches index 4 and we enqueue again,
rear wraps to index 0: rear = (4 + 1) % 5 = 0

This reuses freed space at the beginning.

codeExamples.title: Circular Queue Using Array
codeExamples.explanation: The modulo operation (% MAX) makes the queue circular — when rear reaches the end of the array, it wraps to 0. This reuses space freed by dequeue operations.

commonMistakes: Confusing FIFO (queue) with LIFO (stack)
Not handling the circular wrap-around in circular queues
Forgetting to reset front = rear = -1 when the last element is dequeued
Not checking for full queue before enqueue (causes overwrite)
Using a simple array queue without circular logic — wastes space after dequeues
examTips: Remember FIFO: 'First In, First Out' like a ticket counter line
Know the circular queue formula: rear = (rear + 1) % MAX
Understand the difference between front (where you dequeue) and rear (where you enqueue)
Practice enqueue/dequeue operations step by step
Know applications: CPU scheduling, BFS, printer buffers

practiceQuestions.question: What principle does a queue follow?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A queue follows FIFO (First-In-First-Out). The first element enqueued is the first one dequeued — like a line at a counter.

practiceQuestions.question: In a circular queue of size 5, if front = 3 and rear = 4, how many elements are in the queue?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Elements are at indices 3 and 4. Count = (rear - front + MAX) % MAX + 1 = (4 - 3 + 5) % 5 + 1 = 2. There are 2 elements.

practiceQuestions.question: Which of the following is NOT a typical application of a queue?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Undo functionality uses a STACK (LIFO — you undo the most recent action first). CPU scheduling, BFS, and printer spooling all use queues (FIFO).

lessons.title: Linear Search and Binary Search
lessons.overview: Searching is the process of finding a specific element in a data structure. Linear search checks each element sequentially. Binary search repeatedly halves the search space — but requires the data to be sorted. Choosing the right search algorithm dramatically affects performance.
keyConcepts: Linear Search: check each element from start to end. Works on unsorted data. O(n).
Binary Search: repeatedly divide the sorted array in half. O(log n).
Binary search requires the array to be SORTED first
Binary search compares the middle element, then discards half the array
Best case linear search: O(1) (element is first). Worst case: O(n).
Best case binary search: O(1) (element is the middle). Worst case: O(log n).
formulas: Binary search iterations: log₂(n) — halving until 1 element remains
Linear search comparisons (average): n/2
Binary search: mid = (low + high) / 2

tables.title: Linear Search vs Binary Search
tables.note: For 1 million elements, binary search is ~50,000x faster than linear search in the worst case.

diagrams.title: Binary Search Step-by-Step
diagrams.content:
Array: [2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56, 72, 91]  (sorted)
Search for: 23

Iteration 1: low=0, high=9, mid=4
  arr[4] = 16. 23 > 16, so search right half.
  low = mid + 1 = 5

Iteration 2: low=5, high=9, mid=7
  arr[7] = 56. 23 < 56, so search left half.
  high = mid - 1 = 6

Iteration 3: low=5, high=6, mid=5
  arr[5] = 23. FOUND! Return 5.

3 iterations to find 23 in 10 elements.
Linear search would take 6 iterations.

codeExamples.title: Linear Search
codeExamples.explanation: Simple: loop through the array and compare each element. If found, return the index. If the loop finishes without finding, return -1.

codeExamples.title: Binary Search (Iterative)
codeExamples.explanation: Each iteration halves the search space. After k iterations, the remaining size is n/2^k. The search ends when n/2^k = 1, i.e., k = log₂(n).

commonMistakes: Applying binary search to an unsorted array — it will give wrong results
Using (low + high) / 2 for very large arrays — can overflow. Use low + (high - low) / 2
Forgetting to update low or high after comparing mid
Not handling the case where the element is not found (return -1)
examTips: Always sort before binary search
Binary search is O(log n) — much faster than linear search O(n) for large n
Practice tracing binary search step by step with a small array
Know the overflow-safe mid calculation: mid = low + (high - low) / 2

practiceQuestions.question: Binary search requires the array to be:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Binary search works by comparing the middle element and discarding half. This only works if the array is sorted — otherwise you can't know which half to discard.

practiceQuestions.question: What is the maximum number of comparisons needed to find an element in a sorted array of 1024 elements using binary search?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Binary search halves each iteration. log₂(1024) = 10. So at most 10 comparisons are needed.

practiceQuestions.question: Which search is better for a small array (n < 20)?
options: Linear search — overhead of binary search isn't worth it for small n
practiceQuestions.explanation: For very small arrays, linear search can be faster because binary search has overhead (computing mid, branching). For n < 20, linear search's simplicity often wins.

lessons.title: Bubble, Selection, and Insertion Sort
lessons.overview: Sorting arranges elements in ascending or descending order. Bubble sort repeatedly swaps adjacent elements. Selection sort finds the minimum and places it first. Insertion sort builds the sorted array one element at a time. All three are O(n²) in the worst case but differ in their best-case behavior and number of swaps.
keyConcepts: Bubble Sort: repeatedly compare adjacent pairs, swap if out of order. Largest element 'bubbles up' to the end each pass.
Selection Sort: find the minimum element in the unsorted portion, swap it with the first unsorted element.
Insertion Sort: take each element and insert it into its correct position in the sorted portion (like sorting playing cards).
All three have O(n²) worst-case time complexity
Bubble sort and insertion sort are O(n) best case (already sorted). Selection sort is always O(n²).
Selection sort does the fewest swaps: O(n). Bubble sort does O(n²) swaps.
Insertion sort is stable (preserves order of equal elements). Selection sort is not.
formulas: Bubble sort passes: n-1. Comparisons in pass i: n-i-1. Total: n(n-1)/2
Selection sort comparisons: n(n-1)/2. Swaps: n-1 (one per pass).
Insertion sort comparisons: 1 (best) to i (worst) in pass i. Total worst: n(n-1)/2.

tables.title: Comparison of Sorting Algorithms
tables.note: Stable = preserves relative order of equal elements. Merge sort and quick sort are covered in Unit 5.

codeExamples.title: Bubble Sort with Optimization
codeExamples.explanation: The 'swapped' flag is the key optimization. If a full pass happens without any swap, the array is already sorted and we can stop early. This makes the best case O(n).

codeExamples.title: Selection Sort
codeExamples.explanation: Selection sort finds the minimum and swaps it to the front. It always does n-1 swaps total (one per pass), which is the minimum possible for comparison-based sorting.

codeExamples.title: Insertion Sort (Like Sorting Cards)
codeExamples.explanation: Think of sorting playing cards in your hand. Take each new card and insert it into its correct position among the already-sorted cards. Best case (already sorted) is O(n) because the while loop never executes.

commonMistakes: Forgetting that bubble sort needs n-1 passes (not n)
Inner loop in bubble sort: j < n-i-1, NOT j < n-1 (otherwise you re-compare sorted elements)
Selection sort: comparing arr[j] with arr[i] instead of arr[minIndex]
Insertion sort: starting i from 0 instead of 1 (element at index 0 is already 'sorted')
Not knowing which sort is stable and which isn't
examTips: Know all three algorithms: bubble, selection, insertion — all O(n²) worst case
Bubble sort best case is O(n) with the swapped flag optimization
Selection sort does the fewest swaps: n-1 total
Insertion sort is efficient for nearly-sorted data — O(n) best case
Practice tracing each algorithm step by step with a small array

practiceQuestions.question: Which sorting algorithm has the BEST best-case time complexity?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Bubble sort (with the swapped optimization) is O(n) in the best case (already sorted). Selection sort is always O(n²) even if the array is sorted, because it still scans for the minimum.

practiceQuestions.question: How many swaps does selection sort perform in the worst case?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Selection sort performs exactly n-1 swaps (one per pass). This is the minimum possible for comparison-based sorting, making it efficient when swaps are expensive.

practiceQuestions.question: Which sorting algorithm is most like sorting playing cards in your hand?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Insertion sort works exactly like sorting cards: you pick up each new card and insert it into its correct position among the already-sorted cards.

lessons.title: Binary Trees and BST
lessons.overview: A tree is a hierarchical data structure with nodes connected by edges. A binary tree has at most 2 children per node. A Binary Search Tree (BST) is a binary tree where left child < parent < right child. BSTs enable O(log n) search, insertion, and deletion when balanced.
keyConcepts: Root: the top node. Parent: a node with children. Child: a node below a parent. Leaf: a node with no children.
Depth of a node: number of edges from root to the node. Height of a tree: max depth.
Binary Tree: each node has 0, 1, or 2 children.
BST Property: left subtree values < node value < right subtree values
Traversals: Inorder (Left-Root-Right), Preorder (Root-Left-Right), Postorder (Left-Right-Root)
Inorder traversal of a BST gives elements in sorted order
Balanced BST: height ≈ log n → O(log n) operations
Unbalanced BST (worst case): height = n → O(n) operations (degrades to linked list)
formulas: Max nodes at level i: 2ⁱ
Max nodes in tree of height h: 2^(h+1) - 1
Min height of n nodes: ⌊log₂(n)⌋
BST search: compare key with node, go left if smaller, right if larger

tables.title: Tree Traversals
tables.note: Inorder traversal of a BST produces elements in ascending order.

diagrams.title: Binary Search Tree and Traversals
diagrams.content:
50
        /  \
       30   70
      / \   / \
    20  40 60  80

BST Property:
  20 < 30 < 40 < 50 < 60 < 70 < 80

Inorder (Left-Root-Right):
  20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80  ← SORTED!

Preorder (Root-Left-Right):
  50, 30, 20, 40, 70, 60, 80

Postorder (Left-Right-Root):
  20, 40, 30, 60, 80, 70, 50

codeExamples.title: BST Insertion and Inorder Traversal
codeExamples.explanation: Insertion follows the BST property: smaller values go left, larger values go right. Inorder traversal visits left subtree first, then the node, then right subtree — which produces sorted output.

commonMistakes: Inserting duplicates — decide on a policy (ignore, or count them)
Forgetting that BST operations are O(n) in the worst case (unbalanced tree)
Confusing inorder, preorder, and postorder traversal orders
Not freeing tree nodes when deleting (memory leak)
Forgetting the base case (root == NULL) in recursive traversals
examTips: Inorder traversal of a BST ALWAYS gives sorted output — remember this!

practiceQuestions.question:
What is the inorder traversal of this BST?
     50
    /  \
   30   70
  / \
 20  40
practiceQuestions.explanation: Inorder = Left-Root-Right. Start at 50: go left to 30, go left to 20. 20 has no left, so print 20. Back to 30, print 30. Go right to 40, print 40. Back to 50, print 50. Go right to 70, print 70. Result: 20 30 40 50 70.

practiceQuestions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of searching in a BST?
practiceQuestions.explanation: If the BST is completely unbalanced (all nodes on one side — like a linked list), the height is n, and search requires visiting all n nodes — O(n).

practiceQuestions.question: Which traversal of a BST produces elements in ascending order?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Inorder traversal (Left-Root-Right) visits smaller elements first (left subtree), then the node, then larger elements (right subtree). This produces ascending order.
